RedWing MaaS Packages Android Bank Fraud as a Telegram Rental Service

The Hacker News
2026-07-07 11 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A new Android malware operation called RedWing is being rented out on Telegram as a ready-made bank-fraud service. It lets even low-skill criminals take over a victim's phone, steal their banking logins, and capture the one-time codes that protect their accounts. Zimperium's zLabs, which found the operation, says it looks like a new variant of Oblivion, a $300-a-month rent-a-malware tool

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] RedWing dropper delivery: fake ProtonVPN APK and app-store-lookalike download hosts · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] RedWing Android banking trojan C2 beaconing to named panel domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
RedWing Android banking trojan C2 beaconing to named panel domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts corporate DNS/proxy/EDR-network telemetry for resolution of or connection to RedWing MaaS command-and-control panel hosts (redwing.top, redwingqq.top, krusty-crabs.sbs, and the Cloudflare Workers relay api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev). Any managed or BYOD device — including Android endpoints enrolled in MDE — touching these hosts indicates a live RedWing infection phoning home to receive overlay targets, stream the screen, or exfiltrate SMS/OTP data. Rationale: Uses the four RedWing C2/panel hosts (redwing.top, redwingqq.top, krusty-crabs.sbs, api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev) from Zimperium's zLabs IOC bundle — corroborated against the primary vendor blog, distinct from the THN article text. Named C2 domains are the highest-fidelity anchor available since the kit is reskinned and app-name tracking is unreliable. Cross-checked against: • https://zimperium.com/blog/redwing-a-mobile-malware-as-a-service-operation • https://github.com/Zimperium/IOC/tree/master/2026-07-RedWing
ATT&CKT1437.001 T1481
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst detonating a RedWing sample in a corporate malware sandbox that egresses through the same DNS/proxy
  • Automated TI enrichment connector (Anomali/Recorded Future/urlscan) resolving the domains for verification
  • Safe Links / proxy URL-rewrite prefetch resolving a submitted link without user intent
  • DNS sinkhole already redirecting the domain — query is logged but connection is benign
  • Security awareness / red-team exercise seeding the domain internally
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the client device/IP that resolved the C2 host and confirm it is a real user endpoint (especially an enrolled Android/BYOD device) rather than a sandbox or TI scanner; check for repeated/beaconing hits vs a one-off lookup. 2) CONTAIN: Block the four domains at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate or quarantine the offending device via MDM/EDR, and force a corporate credential + banking-app password reset for the user; check for attacker-set call forwarding (*21*) on the carrier account. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the resolved IPs and on the distribution domains (manyrei.live, wmanyrei.icu, yandex-disk.net, offservers.ru) across the estate, and review the device for a recently sideloaded APK with hidden icon and Accessibility grants.
let C2Hosts = dynamic(["redwing.top","redwingqq.top","krusty-crabs.sbs","api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (C2Hosts)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Hosts = dynamic(["redwing.top","redwingqq.top","krusty-crabs.sbs","api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev"]);
union
(DnsEvents
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Name has_any (C2Hosts)
 | project TimeGenerated, Source="DNS", Device=Computer, Client=ClientIP, Indicator=Name),
(CommonSecurityLog
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DestinationHostName has_any (C2Hosts) or RequestURL has_any (C2Hosts)
 | project TimeGenerated, Source="Proxy/FW", Device=SourceHostName, Client=SourceIP, Indicator=coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RedWing dropper delivery: fake ProtonVPN APK and app-store-lookalike download hosts AIDelivery High
Hunts web/proxy/DNS/EDR-network telemetry for contact with the RedWing distribution infrastructure that serves the sideloaded dropper — the fake Proton_VPN.apk on manyrei.live plus the lookalike/typosquat delivery hosts wmanyrei.icu, yandex-disk.net (impersonating Yandex Disk) and offservers.ru. A corporate or managed device fetching an .apk from these hosts marks the initial-access sideload stage before Accessibility abuse and overlay injection begin. Rationale: Anchored on the RedWing distribution URLs from Zimperium's zLabs IOC bundle — manyrei.live/Proton_VPN.apk (the masqueraded ProtonVPN dropper) plus wmanyrei.icu, the Yandex-Disk typosquat yandex-disk.net, and offservers.ru — corroborated by the vendor blog. The literal 'Proton_VPN.apk' filename and the specific hosts are article-specific delivery-stage indicators, and an .apk fetch on a corporate egress is inherently anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://zimperium.com/blog/redwing-a-mobile-malware-as-a-service-operation • https://github.com/Zimperium/IOC/tree/master/2026-07-RedWing
ATT&CKT1660 T1655
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User genuinely searching for Yandex Disk and mistyping to the yandex-disk.net typosquat (visit is still suspicious but not the trojan)
  • Malware analyst/red team downloading the sample for testing through corporate egress
  • URL sandbox/detonation service (proxy DLP, Safe Links) fetching the .apk to scan it
  • Threat-intel connector resolving the distribution domains for enrichment
  • Proxy content-inspection prefetch touching the host without a real user click
Suppression filter
// Sentinel: drop known detonation/scanner egress and require a real client
| where Client !in ("<proxy_sandbox_ip>") // remove line or keep as-is if no sandbox egress IP; alternatively exclude by device
| where Device !has "sandbox" and Device !has "malware-lab"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm whether the request actually retrieved an .apk (check HTTP method/response size and user-agent) and whether the client is a user endpoint versus a scanner; identify the referring phishing/fake-store URL from proxy logs. 2) CONTAIN: Block the distribution domains and the Proton_VPN.apk path at proxy/DNS/firewall, and if an Android device fetched it, isolate via MDM and block sideloading + the default-SMS/Accessibility roles for the app. 3) HUNT: Pivot the client to the C2 detection (redwing.top / redwingqq.top / krusty-crabs.sbs / api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev) to confirm post-install beaconing, and sweep EmailUrlInfo/proxy for other recipients of the same lure link.
let DropHosts = dynamic(["manyrei.live","wmanyrei.icu","yandex-disk.net","offservers.ru"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (DropHosts) or RemoteUrl has "Proton_VPN.apk"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let DropHosts = dynamic(["manyrei.live","wmanyrei.icu","yandex-disk.net","offservers.ru"]);
union
(CommonSecurityLog
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DestinationHostName has_any (DropHosts) or RequestURL has_any (DropHosts) or RequestURL has "Proton_VPN.apk"
 | project TimeGenerated, Source="Proxy/FW", Device=SourceHostName, Client=SourceIP, Indicator=coalesce(RequestURL, DestinationHostName)),
(DnsEvents
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Name has_any (DropHosts)
 | project TimeGenerated, Source="DNS", Device=Computer, Client=ClientIP, Indicator=Name)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

let LookbackDays = 7d;

          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)

| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

Rogue Agent Flaw Could Have Let Attackers Hijack Google Dialogflow CX Chatbots

The Hacker News
2026-07-07 13 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A critical flaw in Google's Dialogflow CX could have let an attacker with edit rights on one Code Block-enabled agent compromise other Code Block-enabled agents in the same Google Cloud project. From there, they could read live conversations, steal the data users shared, and make the bots send attacker-written messages, including requests to re-enter a password. Security firm Varonis found it

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] IAM grant of Dialogflow edit rights (dialogflow.playbooks.update) — Rogue Agent pre-condition
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Dialogflow CX runtime exceptions revealing malicious Code Block execution · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Rogue Agent Flaw Could Have Let Attackers Hijack Google Dialogflow CX Chatbots
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Dialogflow CX Code Block hijack: UpdatePlaybook DATA_WRITE from anomalous developer identity · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Dialogflow CX Code Block hijack: UpdatePlaybook DATA_WRITE from anomalous developer identity AIInstallation High
Hunts the Varonis 'Rogue Agent' entry point — the dialogflow.playbooks.update permission being exercised via the UpdatePlaybook API, which is the ONLY customer-visible trace of an attacker injecting a malicious Code Block. Surfaces every playbook update with the calling principal, source IP and project so analysts can spot updates from compromised dev accounts or insiders acting off-hours / from new IPs. Rationale: Uses the exact GCP audit methodName google.cloud.dialogflow.cx.v3(beta1).Playbooks.UpdatePlaybook mapped to the dialogflow.playbooks.update permission (DATA_WRITE) named in the article as the whole entry point; method name confirmed against Google Cloud Dialogflow CX audit-logging docs. Sentinel/Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty — this telemetry is GCP audit logs with no equivalent in those platforms' canonical schemas. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/gcp-dialogflow-vulnerability/ • https://docs.cloud.google.com/dialogflow/cx/docs/concept/audit-logging
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1648
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Chatbot developers legitimately editing Playbooks or Code Blocks during business hours
  • CI/CD service accounts pushing agent updates via Terraform / gcloud
  • Bulk playbook migrations across environments (dev→prod promotion)
  • Vendor / consultant accounts with temporary edit rights doing approved changes
Suppression filter
| search NOT "data.protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail"="*gserviceaccount.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the principalEmail + callerIp for the UpdatePlaybook event; confirm the identity is a known Dialogflow developer and the IP/time matches their baseline. Diff the updated Code Block against the approved version in the console (attacker may have restored the console copy while the runtime file stays overwritten). 2) Contain: if the principal or IP is unrecognized, revoke dialogflow.playbooks.update / the Dialogflow editor role from that account, rotate its credentials, and force-redeploy affected agents to reset the shared Cloud Run container. 3) Hunt: enumerate every account/role holding dialogflow.playbooks.update project-wide, review all UpdatePlaybook events from the same principal/IP, and check Dialogflow runtime error logs for Code Block exceptions.

Dialogflow CX runtime exceptions revealing malicious Code Block execution AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the second article-recommended check: failed Dialogflow requests whose error messages leak Python exceptions thrown by an injected/overwritten Code Block (e.g. urllib egress to an attacker server, or a botched code_execution_env.py overwrite). Surfaces ERROR-severity Dialogflow API events so analysts can read the exception text a malicious block produces. Rationale: Directly implements the article's 'run a Cloud Logging query for failed user requests, where the error messages can reveal exceptions thrown by malicious Code Blocks' guidance, scoped to serviceName dialogflow.googleapis.com and ERROR/non-zero status. GCP-only telemetry, so non-GCP query fields are intentionally empty; Sigma skipped because triage depends on reading free-text exception messages rather than a single fixed field match. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/gcp-dialogflow-vulnerability/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/rogue-agent-flaw-could-have-let.html
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1648
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine bugs in developer-written Code Blocks throwing Python exceptions
  • Malformed end-user input causing input-validation code to raise
  • Dialogflow webhook/tool timeouts unrelated to Code Blocks
  • Transient GCP service errors (503/quota) returned to the caller
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the error_messages / status.message text for Python tracebacks referencing urllib, requests, socket, open('code_execution_env.py'), or unexpected external hostnames. Correlate the affected project/agent with any recent UpdatePlaybook event. 2) Contain: if a traceback shows outbound network or file-overwrite behaviour, disable the offending agent's Code Blocks, redeploy to reset the shared container, and open a case with Google Cloud support (the overwrite lives in Google-managed infra). 3) Hunt: pull all UpdatePlaybook events for that project, review who holds dialogflow.playbooks.update, and search for repeated identical exceptions indicating a persistent injected block.

| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values("data.protoPayload.methodName") as methods values("data.protoPayload.status.message") as error_messages values("data.protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp") as src_ip by "data.resource.labels.project_id" "data.protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail"
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
IAM grant of Dialogflow edit rights (dialogflow.playbooks.update) — Rogue Agent pre-condition AIWeaponization Medium
Hunts new IAM bindings that hand an identity a role carrying dialogflow.playbooks.update (roles/dialogflow.admin, roles/dialogflow.consoleAgentEditor / API editor), the single permission that turns a content-edit right into arbitrary Python execution in the shared Code Block runtime. Flags who granted it, to whom, and in which project. Rationale: Targets the article's 'audit which roles and accounts hold dialogflow.playbooks.update' guidance by detecting the moment such a role is granted via SetIamPolicy policyDelta bindingDeltas (standard GCP IAM audit structure). Dialogflow-specific roles keep FP low; GCP-only telemetry so non-GCP fields are empty and Sigma is skipped (policyDelta binding-role match is awkward as a single-field selection across GCP Sigma taxonomies). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/rogue-agent-flaw-could-have-let.html • https://docs.cloud.google.com/dialogflow/cx/docs/concept/audit-logging
ATT&CKT1098.003
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Onboarding a new chatbot developer to a Dialogflow project
  • IaC (Terraform) applying a project's baseline IAM policy
  • Org admin granting a support vendor temporary Dialogflow access
  • Group-based role assignment during a team reorg
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the granting principal is authorized to change IAM and that the grantee is a legitimate Dialogflow developer; check whether the grant coincided with an out-of-hours or new-IP session. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, remove the binding, disable/rotate the grantee and grantor credentials, and review any UpdatePlaybook events made by the grantee since the grant. 3) Hunt: enumerate all current holders of dialogflow.playbooks.update across every project, alert on any that are service accounts or external identities, and baseline expected Dialogflow editors so future grants stand out.

CLOUD

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

logsource:
    category: file_access

detection:

        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

| order by files desc

DEBULL Tooling Abuses Microsoft Device-Code Flow to Target M365 Accounts

The Hacker News
2026-07-07 19 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A Microsoft 365 device code phishing campaign has been observed leveraging collaboration-themed lures to take control of victim accounts between the last week of June 2026 and into early July, per findings from ZeroBEC. "The campaign did not depend on a fake Microsoft password page. It used a malicious collaboration-style lure to push users into the legitimate Microsoft device login experience,

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound collaboration lure linking to DEBULL device-code orchestrator · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] M365 device-code flow sign-in (Storm-2372/DEBULL token theft) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Attacker device registration / PRT persistence via Auth Broker after device-code · [LLM] Illicit OAuth consent to high-privilege Graph scopes (post device-code ATO) · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Endpoint DNS/network connection to DEBULL C2 (pamconj.com / workers.dev) · [LLM] Device-code Auth Broker token replayed from multiple countries · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Bulk M365 mail/file access within 30 min of device-code sign-in · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
M365 device-code flow sign-in (Storm-2372/DEBULL token theft) AIExploitation High
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins that used the OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant ('deviceCodeFlow') from the desktop/mobile client stack - the core DEBULL/Storm-2372 credential-access step where a victim types an attacker-generated user code and hands the attacker a refresh token, bypassing MFA. Device-code auth is rare and near-always attacker-initiated in enterprise M365. Rationale: Device-code flow (originalTransferMethod=deviceCodeFlow, ClientAppUsed=Mobile Apps and Desktop clients) is the single highest-fidelity marker of this whole campaign class; the Microsoft Authentication Broker AppId 29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e is the exact client ID Storm-2372/DEBULL adopted to mint PRTs. Cross-checked Microsoft's Storm-2372 blog, MSTIC's advisory, and Wiz's Entra detection query. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/05/29/defending-against-evolving-identity-attack-techniques/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/debull-tooling-abuses-microsoft-device.html
ATT&CKT1528 T1621 T1566.002
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code sign-ins from genuinely input-constrained devices (smart TVs, conference-room/IoT displays, printers) enrolling into M365
  • Developers/IT running Azure CLI 'az login --use-device-code' or PowerShell Connect-MgGraph -UseDeviceCode for automation and scripting
  • Kiosk or shared-terminal onboarding flows that use device-code to avoid typing passwords on public devices
  • Security researchers or red-team exercises replaying device-code flows in a sanctioned test tenant
  • First-time Authenticator/Company Portal registration on a personal phone where the desktop client stack is reported
Suppression filter
| where not(UserAgent has_any ("AzureCLI","Az-Cli","PowerShell")) // better: join to a 14-day per-user baseline of Country+UserAgent and keep only first-seen combinations
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the sign-in - is the IP/UserAgent/country consistent with the user's baseline? A 'scripty' UserAgent (python-requests, WinHTTP, node) or a country the user never signs in from + Microsoft Authentication Broker AppId is near-certain malicious. Check whether the same sessionId shows two different UserAgents/countries (browser prompt vs backend poller). 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions'), disable the account or force password reset, and enable a Conditional Access policy blocking device-code flow for this user group. 3) HUNT: Search AuditLogs for any new device registration or Authenticator/PRT provisioning tied to this user in the next hours (see the device-registration UC), and enumerate mailbox/SharePoint access from the resulting token session.

| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "deviceCodeFlow"
| where ClientAppUsed == "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients"
| where ErrorCode in (0, 50199)
| extend IsAuthBroker = ApplicationId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, ApplicationId, Application, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed, ErrorCode, IsAuthBroker
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "deviceCodeFlow"
| where ClientAppUsed == "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients"
| where ResultType in ("0", "50199")
| extend IsAuthBroker = AppId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e"   // Microsoft Authentication Broker - Storm-2372/DEBULL PRT pivot
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserDisplayName, AppId, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed, ResultType, IsAuthBroker
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Attacker device registration / PRT persistence via Auth Broker after device-code AIInstallation High
Hunts the DEBULL/Storm-2372 persistence step: the Microsoft Authentication Broker client (29d9ed98-...) using the stolen refresh token to request a token for the Device Registration Service, then registering an attacker-controlled device to obtain a Primary Refresh Token. Article-specific because it keys on the exact broker AppId targeting device-registration resources. Rationale: Uses the exact Microsoft Authentication Broker AppId (29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e) requesting device-registration resources - the precise refresh-token->PRT persistence path MSTIC called out for Storm-2372 and that DEBULL/ARToken automate. Legitimate broker traffic almost never targets Device Registration Service from an interactive user's stolen session. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/05/29/defending-against-evolving-identity-attack-techniques/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/

  • Corporate BYOD onboarding via Company Portal from a sanctioned IP range
  • Intune device re-registration after an OS rebuild or hardware refresh
  • IT-driven bulk device enrollment during a fleet rollout
  • Conditional Access-driven re-registration prompts on a compliant managed device

| where DeviceTrustType != "Azure AD joined" and DeviceTrustType != "Hybrid Azure AD joined"   // sanctioned corporate joins are usually AADJ/HAADJ; attacker workprint devices register as Azure AD registered from unusual IPs

1) TRIAGE: Correlate this device-registration sign-in with the user's device-code sign-in (prior UC) on the same day; confirm the source IP/country is not the user's managed corporate network. Check AuditLogs 'Register device'/'Add registered owner to device' for a brand-new deviceId. 2) CONTAIN: In Entra, disable/delete the newly registered device object, revoke the user's sessions and PRTs, and quarantine the account. Add a Conditional Access require-compliant-device + block device-code policy. 3) HUNT: Enumerate Graph/Exchange access from the attacker device over the following days, review inbox rules and SharePoint/OneDrive downloads, and check whether the compromised mailbox was used to send fresh device-code lures to internal contacts (ATO jumping).

Inbound collaboration lure linking to DEBULL device-code orchestrator AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound emails whose URLs point at DEBULL infrastructure (pamconj.com C2/panel, the Cloudflare Workers lure) or at microsoft.com/devicelogin under payment/shared-folder pretexts - the delivery stage that pushes victims into the real Microsoft device-login prompt. Article-specific via the ZeroBEC/Talos domains. Rationale: Anchors on the ZeroBEC/Talos-confirmed DEBULL domains (spx/dashboard-bl.pamconj.com C2+panel, clear90489058903-document.workers.dev Cloudflare Worker lure) plus microsoft.com/devicelogin in inbound mail - the eSentire-noted culmination point of device-code lures. Dropped frenksv.sbs (only the original article cites it). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/07/01/eviltokens-device-code-phishing-kit-totally-more-evil-than-we-all-thought/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/debull-tooling-abuses-microsoft-device.html

  • Vendor onboarding mail that references Microsoft device authentication for a shared kiosk

| where not (SenderMailFromDomain endswith "microsoft.com" and Url startswith "https://microsoft.com/devicelogin")   // suppress genuine MS-originated device-login mail; DEBULL lures ride external/compromised senders

Check DeliveryAction - if 'Delivered'/'DeliveredAsSpam', who received it and did any click (UrlClickEvents)? 2) CONTAIN: Soft-delete/purge the message tenant-wide via Explorer, block the sender + the DEBULL domains at the mail gateway and network proxy, and add the domains to the TI indicator list. 3) HUNT: Pivot recipients into the device-code sign-in UC to catch any who completed the flow; check whether an already-compromised internal mailbox originated the lure (ATO jumping) by looking for the same URL in outbound/intra-org mail.

Endpoint DNS/network connection to DEBULL C2 (pamconj.com / workers.dev) AICommand & Control High
Hunts endpoint DNS resolutions or connections to the confirmed DEBULL device-code broker/orchestrator infrastructure - spx.pamconj.com (C2 API), dashboard-bl.pamconj.com (operator panel), and the clear90489058903-document.workers.dev lure. Any corporate host reaching this infrastructure indicates a user progressing through the lure or a beaconing session. Rationale: Uses the three ZeroBEC/Talos-corroborated DEBULL domains (spx.pamconj.com C2, dashboard-bl.pamconj.com panel, clear90489058903-document.workers.dev Worker lure). Direct IOC match on infrastructure means any hit is high-confidence; dropped frenksv.sbs as uncorroborated. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/07/01/eviltokens-device-code-phishing-kit-totally-more-evil-than-we-all-thought/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/debull-tooling-abuses-microsoft-device.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security tooling / sandbox detonation deliberately resolving these IOC domains during analysis
  • Threat-intel enrichment services or a SOAR playbook performing passive-DNS lookups from a corporate host
  • A researcher browsing to the panel/lure for investigation from a monitored workstation
  • DNS sinkhole or protective-DNS logging that records the query without an actual connection
  • Stale cached A-record resolution after the domain has been taken down
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe")   // exclude Defender's own IOC-detonation/lookup traffic
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the host + initiating process (browser vs script) and whether an actual TCP/443 connection followed the DNS query. A browser hitting the workers.dev lure means the user is mid-flow; a non-browser process hitting spx.pamconj.com suggests automated token polling. 2) CONTAIN: Block all three domains + resolved IPs at the proxy/firewall and protective DNS, and isolate the host if a non-browser process connected. Force-revoke the associated user's M365 sessions. 3) HUNT: Sweep all DNS/proxy logs org-wide for the same domains to scope other victims, then correlate each source user to the device-code sign-in UC to confirm which completed the token handoff.

Bulk M365 mail/file access within 30 min of device-code sign-in AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a successful device-code flow sign-in to a burst of mailbox/SharePoint/OneDrive read-and-download activity by the same user within 30 minutes - the DEBULL/ARToken/EvilTokens collection-and-exfil stage where the freshly stolen token is immediately used to sweep and export data. Article-specific because it chains the device-code identity event to post-token bulk access. Rationale: Chains the deviceCodeFlow sign-in marker to a >50-action mail/file download burst by the same identity inside 30 minutes - the exact ARToken/EvilTokens SharePoint-exfil + BEC-inbox-sweep behaviour Talos documented, but gated on the device-code root cause so it stays article-specific rather than a generic mass-download rule. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://cyberscoop.com/artoken-bec-platform-cisco-talos/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/
ATT&CKT1114.002 T1530 T1213.002
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately device-code-enrolled kiosk or shared device performing a genuine bulk OneDrive sync on first login
  • A user who signed in via device-code on a new laptop and triggered a full OneDrive/SharePoint client resync
  • eDiscovery or compliance export coinciding with a sanctioned device-code session
  • Backup/migration tooling authenticated via device-code performing mailbox/file bulk reads
  • A power user who habitually opens dozens of documents right after logging in
Suppression filter
| where ActionType != "FileSyncDownloadedFull"   // optional: drop first-login OneDrive full-client resyncs, which dominate benign bulk-download volume
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the device-code sign-in itself was suspicious (foreign IP/scripty UA/Auth Broker) - if benign the download burst is likely a resync. List the DistinctObjects and IPs; downloads from a different IP than the sign-in is a strong exfil signal. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the user's tokens/sessions, disable the account, and if SharePoint sites were swept, apply site-level sharing locks and review external-sharing changes. 3) HUNT: Enumerate any newly created inbox forwarding/delete rules, OAuth consents, and outbound mail from the mailbox; check whether the same downloaded documents were re-shared externally or attached to outbound BEC mail.
let DeviceCodeUsers = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "deviceCodeFlow"
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | summarize DeviceCodeSignInTime = min(Timestamp) by AccountObjectId, AccountUpn;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","FileAccessed","MailItemsAccessed")
| join kind=inner DeviceCodeUsers on AccountObjectId
| where Timestamp between (DeviceCodeSignInTime .. DeviceCodeSignInTime + 30m)
| summarize Actions = count(), DistinctObjects = dcount(ObjectName), FirstAction = min(Timestamp), LastAction = max(Timestamp), SrcIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 5) by AccountObjectId, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, ActionType, DeviceCodeSignInTime
| where Actions > 50   // 50 = bulk-read burst; tune to P99 per-user 30-min access baseline
| order by Actions desc
let DeviceCodeUsers = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "deviceCodeFlow"
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | summarize DeviceCodeSignInTime = min(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName;
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Operation in ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","MailItemsAccessed","SearchQueryPerformed")
| join kind=inner DeviceCodeUsers on $left.UserId == $right.UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (DeviceCodeSignInTime .. DeviceCodeSignInTime + 30m)
| summarize Actions = count(), FirstAction = min(TimeGenerated), LastAction = max(TimeGenerated), SrcIPs = make_set(ClientIP, 5) by UserId, Operation, DeviceCodeSignInTime
| where Actions > 50   // 50 = bulk-read burst; tune to P99 per-user 30-min access baseline
| order by Actions desc
Device-code Auth Broker token replayed from multiple countries AICommand & Control Medium
Flags a Microsoft Authentication Broker (29d9ed98-...) token/session used successfully from two or more countries within a 7-day window - the DEBULL/ARToken persistence-and-abuse pattern where the operator's backend poller and the victim's own device authenticate on the same stolen refresh token from geographically distant IPs. Article-specific via the Auth Broker AppId pivot. Rationale: Pivots on the Microsoft Authentication Broker AppId (29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e) and impossible-travel geo fan-out on non-interactive sign-ins - the observable footprint of the article's 'backend broker generated and polled Microsoft Authentication Broker device-code tokens' while the victim device also uses the same token. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user genuinely travelling and re-authenticating the Authenticator/broker from two countries in a week
  • VPN/egress-gateway hopping that presents the same user's traffic from different national exit IPs
  • Mobile roaming where carrier NAT geolocates sessions to a neighbouring country
  • Cross-border commuters (border-region offices) legitimately signing in from two countries
  • A shared service/test account intentionally exercised from multiple regions
Suppression filter
| where IPCount >= 2 and CountryCount >= 2   // require distinct IPs too; single-IP geo-flapping from one carrier is usually benign
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the per-country IPs and timestamps - if two countries are hit within minutes/hours with different UserAgents (e.g. victim mobile app vs a datacenter/hosting ASN poller), it is token replay, not travel. Confirm whether a device-code sign-in preceded the first country's session. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the user's refresh tokens and sessions, disable the account, and force MFA re-registration; block the hosting/datacenter IP ranges. 3) HUNT: Trace what the token accessed in each region (mail, SharePoint, Graph), enumerate any consent grants or inbox rules created during the window, and check for the same broker AppId + multi-geo pattern across other users to scope the campaign.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ApplicationId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e"   // Microsoft Authentication Broker
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where isnotempty(Country)
| summarize CountryCount = dcount(Country), Countries = make_set(Country, 10), IPCount = dcount(IPAddress), UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn
| where CountryCount >= 2   // same broker token authenticating from 2+ countries in 7d = impossible-travel token replay
| order by CountryCount desc
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AppId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e"   // Microsoft Authentication Broker
| where ResultType == "0"
| extend Ctry = tostring(parse_json(tostring(Location)).countryOrRegion)
| where isnotempty(Ctry)
| summarize CountryCount = dcount(Ctry), Countries = make_set(Ctry, 10), IPCount = dcount(IPAddress), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName
| where CountryCount >= 2   // impossible-travel replay of the device-code-issued broker token
| order by CountryCount desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @properties.appId:29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" (@properties.status.errorCode:0)
Illicit OAuth consent to high-privilege Graph scopes (post device-code ATO) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts consent grants to OAuth applications requesting mail/file/directory read-write scopes (Mail.ReadWrite, Files.ReadWrite.All, Directory.Read.All, offline_access) - the DEBULL/GraphSpy post-authentication persistence path where the hijacked account is used to authorize a long-lived, MFA-independent app foothold via Microsoft Graph. Article-specific to the GraphSpy-derived post-exploitation layer named in the report. Rationale: Targets the GraphSpy/GraphSpy-derived post-authentication layer the article attributes to DEBULL: consent grants to Mail.ReadWrite / Files.ReadWrite.All / Directory.Read.All / offline_access are exactly the scopes needed to exfiltrate mail and files and maintain MFA-independent access via Microsoft Graph after the device-code token theft. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/debull-tooling-abuses-microsoft-device.html • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/05/29/defending-against-evolving-identity-attack-techniques/
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.003
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate onboarding of a sanctioned SaaS app that genuinely needs Mail/Files scopes (e.g. an email-signature or backup vendor)
  • Admin-consent workflows for verified-publisher apps during an approved rollout
  • Developers registering and consenting to their own test apps with offline_access
  • Microsoft first-party apps requesting Directory.Read.All during a feature enablement
  • A migration tool granted Files.ReadWrite.All for a one-time data move
Suppression filter
| where ObjectName !in~ ("Microsoft Graph","Office 365 Exchange Online")   // optional: exclude first-party MS resources; keep third-party/unverified app consents in scope
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the app - is it a verified publisher, how old is the registration, who consented, and from what IP? A brand-new/unverified app consented to right after a device-code sign-in from a foreign IP is high-confidence malicious. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the app's service-principal grants and delete the OAuth2PermissionGrant, revoke the consenting user's sessions, and require admin consent for future grants (disable user consent). 3) HUNT: Review Graph sign-ins by that service principal for mail/file access, correlate the consenting user to the device-code sign-in and multi-geo token UCs, and search for other users who consented to the same appId to scope the campaign.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add app role assignment to service principal.","Add delegated permission grant.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.")
| where RawEventData has_any ("Mail.ReadWrite","Mail.Read","Mail.Send","Files.ReadWrite.All","Files.Read.All","Directory.Read.All","offline_access","MailboxSettings.ReadWrite")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, ActionType, ObjectName, IPAddress, UserAgent, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in ("Consent to application", "Add delegated permission grant", "Add app role assignment to service principal", "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant")
| where tostring(TargetResources) has_any ("Mail.ReadWrite","Mail.Read","Mail.Send","Files.ReadWrite.All","Files.Read.All","Directory.Read.All","offline_access","MailboxSettings.ReadWrite")
| extend Actor = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, TargetResources, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
