Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-

    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

            - 'invoke-expression'

            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    category: file_access
    product: windows

            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'

        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Authentication & network activity from court-filing operator proxy IPs · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ngrok / Teleport tunneling binary execution · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ngrok / Teleport tunneling service resolution & egress (Scattered Spider C2) · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Inbound extortion email matching campaign subject string · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
ngrok / Teleport tunneling service resolution & egress (Scattered Spider C2) AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS/network egress to ngrok and Teleport (teleport.sh) tunneling infrastructure, the exact remote-access tunnels this Scattered Spider cell used to hold access and exfiltrate 77 GB during the May 2025 jewelry-retailer intrusion. Article-specific because both named tools plus the ngrok dashboard domain are cited IOCs. Rationale: ngrok and Teleport are named verbatim in the article as the two tunneling tools; dashboard.ngrok.com is a listed IOC and teleport.sh is confirmed by Darktrace/ReliaQuest as the 77 GB exfil channel. Domain resolution to these services from a corporate endpoint is high-signal where neither tool is sanctioned. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/untangling-the-web-darktraces-investigation-of-scattered-spiders-evolving-tactics • https://reliaquest.com/blog/scattered-spider-attack-analysis-account-compromise/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090 T1567.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately using ngrok to expose a local dev service
  • IT team piloting Teleport (goteleport.com) for sanctioned bastion/SSH access
  • QA/webhook testing tunnels to ngrok for integration work
  • Security researchers detonating malware in a sandbox that beacons to ngrok
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\dev\", @"\repos\", @"\source\") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-devtunnel"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and user on the resolving host; confirm whether ngrok/Teleport is sanctioned software for that team. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, kill the tunnel process, and block ngrok/teleport.sh domains at the proxy/firewall; force-reset the involved account and its MFA. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for the tunnel binaries (ngrok.exe/tsh.exe), large outbound transfers to amazonaws.com/S3, and help-desk-driven password/MFA resets in the prior 72h.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("ngrok.io","ngrok-free.app","ngrok-free.dev","ngrok.app","ngrok.com","teleport.sh")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Count=count(), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("ngrok.io","ngrok-free.app","ngrok-free.dev","ngrok.app","ngrok.com","teleport.sh")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), Queries=make_set(DnsQuery,10) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: ngrok or Teleport Tunneling Service DNS Resolution
id: 5f1c3a08-2d94-4c1e-9c7a-8b2e5a4d1f01

NETWORK

| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`

ngrok / Teleport tunneling binary execution AIInstallation High
Detects execution of the ngrok agent (ngrok.exe) or Teleport client (tsh.exe / teleport.exe), including tell-tale command lines (ngrok tcp/http/authtoken, tsh login). This is the on-host install/run step of the tunnels used to keep access and stage the 77 GB exfil in the May 2025 intrusion. Rationale: Both ngrok and Teleport are explicitly named; the ngrok.exe agent and Teleport tsh.exe client with their canonical subcommands (tcp/http/authtoken/login) are precise, low-FP execution artifacts distinct from the network pivot in UC1. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://reliaquest.com/blog/scattered-spider-attack-analysis-account-compromise/
ATT&CKT1572 T1219 T1567.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running ngrok.exe for a local webhook demo
  • IT admin using tsh.exe against a sanctioned Teleport cluster
  • CI/CD runner invoking ngrok for ephemeral test tunnels
  • Renamed-but-legit portable ngrok in a user's Downloads for a hackathon
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe","devenv.exe") and AccountName in~ ("builduser","ci-runner"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary path, signer, and whether the running user/team is authorized to use ngrok/Teleport; capture the full command line and any authtoken. 2) Contain: kill the process, isolate the host, block the tunnel domains, and revoke/reset the executing account plus its MFA enrollment. 3) Hunt: correlate to preceding help-desk password/MFA resets, outbound transfers to amazonaws.com, and DNS to ngrok/teleport.sh across other hosts sharing the same account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("ngrok.exe","tsh.exe","teleport.exe")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ngrok tcp","ngrok http","ngrok authtoken","tsh login","teleport.sh")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ngrok.exe","tsh.exe","teleport.exe")
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ngrok tcp","ngrok http","ngrok authtoken","tsh login","teleport.sh")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inbound extortion email matching campaign subject string AIActions on Objectives Medium
Flags inbound email carrying the attackers' distinctive ransom subject line ('WE STOLE THE DATA', typo 'UMMEDIATELY') sent after the retailer blocked the ransomware and evicted them. The misspelling makes this an extremely low-FP string tied to this specific extortion attempt. Rationale: The ransom email subject 'IMPORTANT: WE STOLE THE DATA, CONTACT UMMEDIATELY [sic]' is quoted verbatim in the article; the 'UMMEDIATELY' misspelling is a near-unique string, so a subject match is high-precision. Sentinel/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty — the signal lives only in mail telemetry (Defender EmailEvents / Splunk Email datamodel), which has no clean equivalent in those platforms. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/court-filing-reveals-windows-device-id.html • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/07/07/windows-is-watching-anti-piracy-tool-fingers-scattered-spider-suspect/5267953
ATT&CKT1657 T1486
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal phishing-simulation exercise reusing the leaked subject line
  • Threat-intel briefing or news forward that quotes the ransom subject in the body/subject
  • Analyst mailing the sample subject to a shared mailbox for triage
Suppression filter
| where DeliveryAction != "Blocked" | where SenderFromDomain !endswith "phishsim.contoso.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full message (sender, headers, SenderIPv4, any crypto wallet / $8M demand) and confirm it is a genuine external extortion note, not a sim or forward. 2) Contain: quarantine the message tenant-wide via the NetworkMessageId, preserve it for IR/legal, and notify incident command — a received extortion note implies data was already staged/taken. 3) Hunt: work backwards for the breach — prior ngrok/Teleport tunnels, 77 GB-class transfers to Amazon S3, and help-desk resets on privileged accounts.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where Subject has_any ("WE STOLE THE DATA","UMMEDIATELY","CONTACT UMMEDIATELY")
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderIPv4, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where Subject has_any ("WE STOLE THE DATA","UMMEDIATELY","CONTACT UMMEDIATELY")
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderIPv4, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where (All_Email.subject="*WE STOLE THE DATA*" OR All_Email.subject="*UMMEDIATELY*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where (All_Email.subject="*WE STOLE THE DATA*" OR All_Email.subject="*UMMEDIATELY*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Authentication & network activity from court-filing operator proxy IPs AIExploitation Medium
Matches sign-ins and outbound connections against the twelve VPN/proxy IPs from the unsealed complaint that the operator used to reach the ngrok signup page and the retailer's site. Use as an IOC sweep for the same infrastructure across the estate, including CloudTrail source IPs for the S3 exfil. Rationale: The twelve proxy IPs are pre-extracted IOCs from the complaint that the device repeatedly surfaced on (ngrok signup, retailer access). They are shared commercial-VPN ranges (mostly 146.70.x M247/DataPacket), hence Medium confidence — a hit warrants investigation but not blind blocking. CloudTrail sweep is included because exfil went to Amazon S3, so these source IPs may appear on PutObject calls. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/court-filing-reveals-windows-device-id.html • https://gbhackers.com/windows-device-track-scattered-spider-hacking-group-member/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1090
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employee legitimately using the same commercial VPN provider (Mullvad/M247 shared egress) for privacy
  • Traveling user routed through a VPN concentrator on an overlapping IP
  • Threat-intel scanner or researcher pivoting from the same VPN range
  • IP re-allocated to a benign tenant since the May 2025 activity (shared-IP staleness)
Suppression filter
| where ResultType == 0 and UserAgent !has "Mullvad" | where AppDisplayName in~ ("Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Azure Active Directory PowerShell") == false
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit confirm the account, app, and whether the sign-in succeeded; check if the user has any business reason to use that VPN and whether the auth was MFA-satisfied. 2) Contain: for successful privileged sign-ins, revoke sessions, reset credentials + MFA, and add the IPs to a monitored/blocked list (block cautiously — shared VPN). 3) Hunt: from any matched account pivot to ngrok/Teleport execution, S3 uploads, and help-desk reset events; sweep CloudTrail for these IPs on S3/IAM actions.

| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Application, ErrorCode, Country, City, UserAgent
| order by Timestamp desc

| where IPAddress in (iocIPs)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, ResultType, ResultDescription, tostring(Location), UserAgent

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1219
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\AnyDesk.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer_Service.exe'
            - '\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe'
            - '\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe'
            - '\atera_agent.exe'
            - '\SplashtopStreamer.exe'
            - '\RustDesk.exe'
            - '\NinjaOne.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - IT-approved RMM in use across the estate. Maintain a known-IT-
      tool exclusion list per environment.
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EGroupware CVE-2026-27823 arbitrary file read via importexport download path traversal AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the EGroupware importexport export handler carrying a traversal-laden _filename parameter. This is the arbitrary-file-read primitive attackers use to exfiltrate a valid header.inc.php before overwriting it for RCE — article-specific because it pins the exact vulnerable menuaction and parameter. Rationale: Anchors on the exact vulnerable menuaction 'importexport.importexport_export_ui.download' plus a path-traversal _filename token straight from the advisory's PoC URL — the pair is not something benign EGroupware traffic produces. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9qx-v5xp-ph8p • https://www.cvedetails.com/vulnerability-list/vendor_id-2373/Egroupware.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) probing EGroupware with traversal templates
  • Internal pentest or red-team validation of CVE-2026-27823
  • Security researcher testing after patch to confirm remediation
  • WAF in monitor-mode logging blocked-then-passed requests
Suppression filter
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the HTTP status — a 200 with a non-trivial response body means the file read succeeded; extract SrcIpAddr and check whether _filename resolved to header.inc.php or another sensitive file. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source IP at the WAF/edge and confirm EGroupware is patched (>= 26.2.20260224 / >= 23.1.20260224); disable user self-registration if enabled. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same SrcIpAddr for subsequent POST uploads to the SmallPart media recorder and for any modification of header.inc.php on the host.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "menuaction=importexport.importexport_export_ui.download"
| where Url has_any ("_filename=../", "_filename=..%2f", "%2e%2e%2f", "..%5c", "header.inc.php")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EGroupware header.inc.php overwritten by web process (CVE-2026-27823 RCE persistence) AIInstallation High
Detects the web/PHP runtime writing or modifying header.inc.php — EGroupware's core bootstrap config, which is normally only written during setup. In CVE-2026-27823 the auth-bypass file-write primitive overwrites this file with attacker PHP to achieve RCE on restart/OPcache expiry. Rationale: header.inc.php is EGroupware's bootstrap config; a write to it by php/php-fpm/apache at runtime (not during setup) is the exact RCE persistence artifact named in the advisory. Filename + web-process parent make it very high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9qx-v5xp-ph8p
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate EGroupware setup/reconfiguration wizard writing header.inc.php
  • Admin editing config via the setup UI after an upgrade
  • Automated deployment/config-management (Ansible/Puppet) templating header.inc.php — but that runs as a deploy user, not php-fpm
  • Package upgrade regenerating the config file
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup","cli.php","doctrine") )
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Diff the new header.inc.php against a known-good copy; look for injected PHP (system/exec/passthru, base64 blobs, added functions) beyond the expected config array. 2) CONTAIN: Restore header.inc.php from backup, kill the php-fpm/apache workers, and take the host off the network if injected code is present. 3) HUNT: Search DeviceProcessEvents for php-fpm/apache spawning shells or network tools, and review web logs for the preceding SmallPart ajax_upload POST and importexport file-read that seeded the attack.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "header.inc.php"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-fpm","php-fpm8","apache2","httpd","nginx") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/var/www","/usr/share/egroupware")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "header.inc.php"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php","php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EGroupware web runtime (php-fpm/apache) spawning a shell or network tool — CVE-2026-27823 RCE execution AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the PHP/web server process spawning interactive shells or download utilities, the observable execution stage once CVE-2026-27823's poisoned header.inc.php runs. Article-specific because EGroupware executes as www-data under php-fpm/apache, so shell children of that process are anomalous. Rationale: The advisory states EGroupware runs as www-data under the web server and achieves RCE via header.inc.php; a php-fpm/apache parent spawning a shell or curl/wget is the direct execution signature of that RCE, keyed on the runtime's own process names. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9qx-v5xp-ph8p
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EGroupware cron/async jobs invoking php CLI that shells out (e.g. mail delivery, LDAP sync)
  • Server monitoring plugins run under the web user calling id/uname/whoami
  • ImageMagick/document-conversion features legitimately calling helper binaries
  • Deployment hooks or health-checks executed by the web process during restart
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-c ","/tmp/","http://","https://","/dev/tcp","base64","-i")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child — reverse-shell one-liners, curl|bash to external IPs, or recon (id;uname -a) are true-positive; a known EGroupware maintenance task is benign. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, capture the php-fpm/apache process tree, and rotate EGroupware admin/setup credentials (advisory notes setup-password modification as an alternative impact). 3) HUNT: Correlate back to the header.inc.php write and the importexport file-read/SmallPart upload from the same host/IP, and scan for outbound C2 from the web process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-fpm","php-fpm8","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat","whoami","id","uname")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php","php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl","/nc","/ncat","/whoami","/id","/uname")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

ImFileEvent

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Outbound connection to UAT-7810 (LapDogs ORB) SHORTLEASH/DOGLEASH C2 VPS AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any managed host or network device egressing to the four VPS IPs Talos attributes to UAT-7810 for hosting SHORTLEASH/LONGLEASH/DOGLEASH payloads and C2. Because these are dedicated attacker-acquired VPS (not shared CDN/cloud), any connection is high-fidelity and survives across the campaign's HTTP (8088/2222) and TLS (99) services. Rationale: Anchored on the four dedicated VPS IPs (194.233.92.26, 217.15.160.247, 217.15.164.147, 95.182.100.231) and the campaign ports 8088/2222/99 from the article's IOC block; these are attacker-owned relays, so a hit is near-unambiguous. Cross-checked SecurityScorecard's LapDogs report and Expel's ShortLeash hunt for infra continuity. Cross-checked against: • https://securityscorecard.com/blog/unmasking-a-new-china-linked-covert-orb-network-inside-the-lapdogs-campaign/ • https://expel.com/blog/gonzo-threat-hunting-lapdogs-shortleash/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7810/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment / IOC-validation tooling actively probing the listed IPs from a SOC jump box
  • Security researcher or scanner (Shodan/Censys agent) coincidentally connecting from a monitored host
  • VPN or cloud NAT egress where an unrelated tenant transiently used the same VPS IP after reassignment
  • Sinkhole or honeypot infrastructure intentionally beaconing to campaign IPs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("threatintel-enrichment.exe","nmap.exe","masscan.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the source host/device and initiating process/user; confirm whether it is a Linux/embedded network device (Ruckus/ASUS) or a general endpoint, and whether the connection port was 8088/2222/99. 2) Contain: Block the four IPs at the perimeter firewall, isolate the source device, and for network appliances pull config and check for unexpected iptables ACCEPT rules and rogue listeners. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the source to find wget/curl/tftp pulls of ELF payloads (MIPS/ARM/x64), DOGLEASH listener ports, and the LONGLEASH hardcoded User-Agent 'Chrome/122.0.6261.95' in proxy logs; sweep all edge devices for the same egress.

| where RemoteIP in ("194.233.92.26","217.15.160.247","217.15.164.147","95.182.100.231")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog

| where DestinationIP in ("194.233.92.26","217.15.160.247","217.15.164.147","95.182.100.231")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DOGLEASH ELF payload download from UAT-7810 servers on Linux/embedded devices AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the DOGLEASH deployment shell script that uses wget/curl/tftp/busybox to pull multi-arch (MIPS/ARM/x64) ELF payloads directly from UAT-7810's four hosting VPS onto compromised networking/Linux devices. This targets the install step where the attacker downloads-and-executes on the router itself rather than the later C2 beacon. Rationale: Combines the article's DOGLEASH deployment behaviour (shell script downloads the ELF then adds an iptables ACCEPT rule and executes) with the four concrete hosting IPs, so a download utility whose cmdline contains an attacker IP is a precise install-stage signal. Talos states multi-arch DOGLEASH variants were staged on these servers via shell scripts. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7810/ • https://securityscorecard.com/blog/unmasking-a-new-china-linked-covert-orb-network-inside-the-lapdogs-campaign/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.004 T1562.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin/automation fetching firmware or scripts that happens to include one of the IPs (rare given these are attacker VPS)
  • Vulnerability scanner or IR responder pulling the sample from the C2 for analysis onto a lab Linux host
  • Threat-intel harvesting jobs that mirror attacker payloads via curl/wget
  • Package mirror on the same hosting provider transiently reusing the IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "malware-analysis" and FolderPath !startswith "/opt/ir-sandbox/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: On the source device inspect the full download command, the destination file path, and whether the fetched file was chmod'd and executed; capture the ELF and its architecture. 2) Contain: Isolate the device from the network, kill the DOGLEASH process/listener, remove any attacker-added iptables ACCEPT rule (INPUT --dport … -j ACCEPT), and preserve a forensic image. 3) Hunt: Enumerate all edge/IoT devices for the same download pattern, look for the bound listener port and inbound TCP that gets decoded with the hardcoded password, and correlate with egress to the four C2 IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("wget","curl","ftpget","tftp","busybox","ftpput")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("194.233.92.26","217.15.160.247","217.15.164.147","95.182.100.231")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("194.233.92.26","217.15.160.247","217.15.164.147","95.182.100.231")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("wget","curl","ftpget","tftp","busybox")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, ProcessID, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UAT-7810 self-signed 'exploit' TLS certificate served on non-standard port 99 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunting UC for TLS sessions to UAT-7810 VPS on the unusual port 99, where Talos observed a self-signed certificate with subject_dn 'C=exploit, ST=exploit, L=exploit, O=exploit, OU=exploit, CN=exploit' (SHA256 c2ab9adaba93ff094b8f3fc37d906014d870582039d276b7bd03e6fd583d8a15). The cert fingerprint is the pivot that survives IP rotation—use it in Zeek/PCAP to discover unknown infra beyond the listed IPs. Rationale: Uses the article's exact TLS artefacts—port 99, cert SHA256 c2ab9ada… and the distinctive subject_dn where every field equals 'exploit'—as a durable infra fingerprint; the endpoint/firewall queries flag the port-99 hits and the cert values in rationale drive Zeek x509 hunting for un-listed servers. Defender has no certificate telemetry, so cert-fingerprint matching must be done in Zeek ssl.log/x509.log. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7810/ • https://securityscorecard.com/blog/unmasking-a-new-china-linked-covert-orb-network-inside-the-lapdogs-campaign/
ATT&CKT1573.002 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner probing port 99 on the listed IPs during an authorized scan
  • Rare legitimate service that happens to run TLS on port 99 within the org contacting one of these IPs
  • IR/threat-intel host fingerprinting the C2 cert for validation
  • IP reassignment where the VPS later hosts a benign service on port 99
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nmap.exe","masscan.exe","nessus.exe","openssl.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the source host and whether a TLS handshake to port 99 completed; if TLS-inspection/Zeek is available, verify the presented cert matches SHA256 c2ab9ada… or subject O=exploit/CN=exploit. 2) Contain: Block the IPs and port-99 egress, isolate the source, and preserve PCAP of the handshake. 3) Hunt: Extract the cert fingerprint/subject from Zeek x509.log and sweep all TLS metadata for the same self-signed 'exploit' cert on any IP to surface UAT-7810 infrastructure not in the published IOC set; correlate hits with DOGLEASH downloads and the four C2 IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemotePort == 99
| where RemoteIP in ("194.233.92.26","217.15.160.247","217.15.164.147")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationPort == 99
| where DestinationIP in ("194.233.92.26","217.15.160.247","217.15.164.147")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
